headline: A Gentle Pulse in the Ear Offers New Hope for Stubborn High Blood Pressure
meta_description: Researchers at Queen Mary University of London tested a handheld device that stimulates ear nerves to lower blood pressure, showing promise for severe cases.
summary_short: A small device delivering gentle electrical pulses through the ear showed safety and promise for patients with severe hypertension in a new clinical trial.
body:
Researchers at Queen Mary University of London have unveiled an unexpectedly practical approach to tackling high blood pressure: a handheld device no larger than a clip that patients can use at home. In a clinical trial of 63 people whose blood pressure remained stubbornly elevated despite medication, the device proved safe, comfortable, and easy to use. Most importantly, patients with the most severe hypertension experienced meaningful blood pressure reductions when receiving active stimulation—a finding that suggests this non-invasive technology could eventually offer relief to millions for whom standard drugs alone fall short.

The device works through transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation, delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear via two small clips positioned on the tragus, the cartilage flap just in front of the ear canal. Participants used it for 30 minutes daily in the first two weeks, then once weekly for 10 more weeks. While the treatment showed no significant advantage over a sham device when tested across the entire group, the critical finding emerged in a prespecified subgroup analysis: those entering the trial with more severe hypertension saw clear improvements with active stimulation compared to placebo.

Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator at Queen Mary University and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, called it "an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology" that could offer a "cheap, scalable solution for millions." The trial, published in Hypertension, represents the first and most thorough study of its kind. Though larger studies are needed to confirm effectiveness and identify which patients benefit most, the results point toward an encouraging new direction: a simple, surgery-free option that patients control themselves, potentially complementing existing medications for one of the world's most stubborn health challenges.
quick_facts: Handheld device clips onto ear to stimulate blood pressure-regulating nerves
Clinical trial of 63 patients at Queen Mary University of London
Showed promising results in patients with severe, hard-to-control hypertension
Safe, well-tolerated, and practical for daily home use
